summary.value: This paper proposes DR MAMR, a series of enhancements for reinforcement learning algorithms focused on multi-turn multi-agent systems like those introduced in ReMA (Wan 2025). Here, the focus is on multi-agent systems that alternate between a meta-agent, whose purpose is to provide higher-level planning and form intermediate tasks, and a reasoner agent, whose purpose is to reason about and solve tasks proposed by the meta-agent. DR MAMR identifies a “lazy agent” shortcoming in ReMA, where a single agent does all of the planning and reasoning, while the other agent produces short (or no) outputs. The authors then propose fixes to this involving modifications to the loss function and methods for provider denser credit attribution via Shapely values. The authors train models at 3B, 7B, and 14B scale and evaluate on math tasks.

strengths.value:
- Shapely values are an interesting, and to my knowledge, novel way to provide dense credit attribution in multi-turn settings with relatively small computational overhead (a 0.5B embedding model is required to compute semantic similarity). The ablation result shows that such credit attribution has a large impact on performance.
- The proposed changes and additions to the loss and reward formulation are principle and experimentally backed with controlled ablations.
- The paper is generally well-written and the problem of the lazy agent is well-motivated

weaknesses.value:
- Relatively weak baseline choices: The second performing baseline across model scales is GRPO training. There exist many algorithmic improvements on top of GRPO that enable better performance, such as DAPO, DR GRPO. The advantage of these methods is that they do not require such complicated rollout and reward approaches needed by ReMA and DR MAMR. Even a comparison across one model size, like 7B, would be helpful.
- The authors focus only on math domains, eschewing other reasoning domains/benchmarks. As a starting point, I would love to see if DR MAMR models generalize to other domains, e.g., evaluating on GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Pro, etc.
- Theoretical presentation: The proposed theorem is a trivial re-arrangement of the defined $g, Z$ terms. The full proof of this result reveals the simplicity, as it spends the majority of the space deriving the expression for $Z$ (by simply performing some algebraic manipulations involving gradient computations), then concluding with some additional algebraic manipulations. Overall, I find this result overstated: It does not introduce any novel result, nor does it use novel techniques in the proof. Presenting such a result as a standalone theorem needlessly complicates presentation.

questions.value:

- Nit: GRPO stands for Group Relative Policy Optimization, not Preference Optimization (L46)

We sincerely appreciate the reviewer for carefully examining our theoretical section and for the constructive feedback. 

Our idea is that when realistic reward noise is taken into consideration, it becomes difficult to quantitatively compare the exact gradient magnitudes of two trajectories, and thus we intentionally abstract away this confounder. We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. We did conduct an experiment using a process reward model, as reported in **Appendix G**, and apologize for not referencing it clearly in the main text. In this experiment, we followed the setup in Section 6.1 and adopted **Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B** as the process reward model (PRM), adding its process reward to each turn’s reward.

As shown in **Fig. 6 (Appendix)**, this approach collapses rapidly within 30 training steps, which we attribute to **reward hacking**—a common issue when dense process rewards directly evaluate turn-level quality. In contrast, our Shapley-style causal-influence estimator focuses only on each turn’s contribution to the next reasoning step and leaves quality evaluation to the final verifiable reward, thereby avoiding reward hacking and providing more stable credit signals.

summary.value: The paper studies why lazy-agent behavior emerges in multi‑agent LLM reasoning (one agent effectively does all the work while the other contributes little) and proposes a theoretical framework to address this issue by tracing the problem to a bias in multi‑turn GRPO: the turn‑length normalization favors shorter trajectories, implicitly discouraging collaborative back‑and‑forth. Then introduce Dr. MAMR with three components: (i) remove the turn‑length normalization identified by the theory; (ii) add a Shapley‑inspired step‑level causal‑influence signal computed by grouping semantically similar steps across rollouts(which is common is MARL setting); and (iii) add a verifiable reward for restart via a <restart> control that lets the reasoning agent discard noisy history and begin afresh. On seven math benchmarks with Qwen2.5 7B and 14B‑Instruct, Dr. MAMR outperforms single‑agent GRPO, VRP(CoT), and ReMA. And improves stability (ReMA collapses; Dr. MAMR does not).

strengths.value:
-- Motivation: The paper motivates that lazy‑agent behavior collapses multi‑agent systems into single‑agent reasoning, squandering collaboration benefits, which is an issue observed in MARL and newly shown here in LLM multi‑agent reasoning. The motivation is explicit in the introduction and contribution summary.

Well structured: 

-- Crisp theoretical diagnosis of the cause. Theorem 1 in (Sec. 5.1, p. 5) formalizes how the 1/T normalization in multi‑turn GRPO biases the gradient toward shorter (fewer‑turn) continuations with equal final reward, explaining the emergence of lazy agents; the authors also argue the bias is pronounced because turns are far fewer than tokens. (Sec. 5.1, p. 5) 

-- Methodologically well‑scoped fix. The Shapley‑inspired causal‑influence estimator averages masked‑history log‑likelihood deltas over groups of semantically similar steps, reducing phrasing bias and variance. A “who helped whom” question. (Sec. 5.2, p. 6; Appx. B.3, p. 18)

weaknesses.value:
-- Domain generality is narrow. All experiments are on math; claims about “complex reasoning tasks” would be stronger with code, planning, or QA tasks where verifiability is harder. Which can lead to another question:
-- Restart relies on verifiable end‑state. The restart reward needs a checkable final answer; outside math (or without ground‑truth/validators), the mechanism may not be directly applicable. Moreover, ablations show restart helps but less than CI/normalization fixes, suggesting narrower impact. (Sec. 5.3 p. 7; Table 2 p. 9)

-- Theory relies on an equal final reward assumption. Theorem 1 contrasts continuations with equal final reward but different lengths; this is a clean but restrictive setting. It is less clear how strongly the conclusion holds under more realistic reward noise, token‑level normalizations/clipping, or different credit schemes. (Sec. 5.1, p. 5) 

-- Sensitivity of the CI estimator is underexplored. Grouping uses Qwen2.5‑0.5B embeddings and a cosine‑similarity threshold of 0.9; \alpha = \beta = 0.1 are fixed across runs for stability. The paper lacks ablations on embedding choice/threshold and \alpha /\beta, so robustness of CI to these design choices is uncertain. (Appx. B.2–B.3, p. 18)

-- Connection to MARL: Comparative context to prior “lazy‑agent” literature could be tighter. The paper cites MARL work on lazy agents but does not empirically compare to mechanisms from that line (e.g., influence‑based credit or external‑state influence). This limits continuity with prior method. (Sec. 2, p. 3; cf. ICML’23 “Lazy Agents” & Lazy‑MDPs)

Besides the weakness, I have something to ask:

-- Theory stress tests: Beyond removing 1/T, did you try alternatives (e.g., adaptive normalization by effective turns that exclude no‑ops, or per‑role normalization)? Do the theoretical predictions hold when rewards differ slightly (near‑equal) or when token‑level normalizations are active? (Sec. 5.1, p. 5)

-- The phenomenon of “lazy agents” has been studied in MARL (e.g., LAIES at ICML’23; Lazy‑MDPs). This paper’s contribution is to diagnose and mitigate it in multi‑agent LLM reasoning with a targeted loss fix, a tractable step‑level influence signal, and a restart‑credit mechanism. What's your next plan for further work to combine this work?

However, when a deterministic validator is not available, a natural extension of our restart mechanism still applies.

If the reasoning agent outputs restart at turn _t_, we can generate a **counterfactual non-restart continuation** for the same prompt (i.e., force the agent to continue instead of restarting). Both final answers can then be scored by the same reward function—which is already required in all RL settings, including non-verifiable tasks. The restart reward is defined as the improvement in reward-model score obtained by restarting relative to this counterfactual continuation.

This preserves the core principle of our design: **restart is rewarded only when it truly improves the final answer**, regardless of whether the evaluator is a deterministic math verifier or a learned reward model. Therefore, the mechanism naturally generalizes beyond math and remains applicable to any RL setting where a reward model or evaluator is available.

The core difficulty is that MARL counterfactual methods assume a small, discrete action space, where one can enumerate or approximate how an agent’s alternative action would change the joint outcome. In LLM multi-agent reasoning, however, an “action’’ is an entire natural-language message, and even a single-token modification can drastically alter the downstream reasoning of the other agent. Constructing semantically plausible counterfactual actions is therefore non-trivial, and evaluating their impact becomes intractable.

  

In addition, previous MARL counterfactual-influence methods aim to measure how a different action would have changed another agent’s action. Our objective is fundamentally different: we quantify how the agent’s actual message contributes to the current intermediate state of the reasoning trajectory.

  

Thus, while the high-level phenomenon is related, existing MARL lazy-agent solutions cannot be directly applied to multi-agent LLM reasoning. We appreciate the reviewer for highlighting this connection and will incorporate this clarification into the related-work discussion.

A key empirical observation (Fig. 5) already reveals the fundamental issue: trajectories exhibiting lazy-agent behavior are typically shorter. This is intuitive—once an agent becomes lazy, it stops contributing and the interaction terminates earlier. Under any length-based normalization, these shorter trajectories inevitably receive larger gradient weights simply because their denominators are smaller.

  

- **Effective-turn normalization**. Removing no-op or blank turns does not alleviate this asymmetry. Lazy trajectories typically contain more low-content turns; filtering them out makes their effective length even shorter, whereas well-reasoned trajectories retain most turns. As a result, effective-turn normalization may actually amplify the weight advantage of lazy trajectories.

  

- **Per-role normalization**. Normalizing per agent simply rescales contributions but does not change the ordering: lazy trajectories still give each agent fewer turns and therefore a smaller denominator. Well-reasoned trajectories remain down-weighted because their cooperative exchange inherently requires more turns.

We thank the reviewer for raising this concern. We respectfully clarify that the lazy-agent phenomenon is _not_ specific to ReMA, but arises from a _general structural property_ of multi-agent RL systems when rewards are assigned only on the final outcome.

- **(i) Lazy-agent collapse is a well-known failure mode in multi-agent RL literature**: Prior work in multi-agent RL has documented that when multiple agents share a _single global reward_, individual agents tend to free-ride on the others [1][2], leading to _lazy_ or _inactive_ policies. The core reason is: **credit assignment is ambiguous when every agent receives the same final reward.**

- **(ii) The issue is not specific to ReMA — it arises whenever multi-agent systems use R1-style training**: The lazy-agent behavior does not stem from the ReMA architecture itself. Instead, it arises from the **reward structure induced by R1-based RL**, which has become _widely adopted and empirically effective_ in reasoning-oriented RL following DeepSeek-R1. Because only the _final_ answer is verifiable, every agent in a multi-agent system receives **the same terminal reward**, regardless of its individual contribution. This inherently makes credit assignment ambiguous and naturally encourages laziness.

- **This mechanism is shared by any multi-agent LLM system trained with R1-style rewards**, whether the interaction pattern is planner–solver, supervisor–worker, debate, or CoT+verifier. The architectural details differ, but the credit-assignment limitation is identical whenever training relies on a single verifiable final reward.

---------

>### **(2) our solution is framework-agnostic and plug-and-play for a broad family of multi-agent LLM systems**

We appreciate the reviewer’s concern. However, our contributions are **not tied to the ReMA architecture** and are intentionally designed to be **framework-agnostic** and **plug-and-play** for a broad family of multi-agent LLM systems.

- **(i) the training objective used by ReMA—multi-turn GRPO—is _not_ unique to ReMA**. Multi-turn GRPO and its variants have recently been adopted widely in LLM RL, including multi-agent settings and multi-turn single-agent RL [3][4][5][6][7]. Our theoretical analysis identifies a fundamental bias in the turn-normalization term that inherently favors shorter trajectories over longer but equally rewarded ones. This insight is applicable to **any** framework built upon multi-turn GRPO, and provides guidance for future multi-agent and multi-turn RL designs beyond ReMA itself.

- **(ii) our Shapley-inspired causal-influence estimator is not tied to the ReMA architecture, nor does it _require_ any specialized multi-agent structure.** Rather, it can be **naturally adapted** to the widely adopted interaction pattern in modern LLM multi-agent systems, where agents communicate **sequentially** and jointly produce a single final answer.

- **(iii) we propose a novel restart deliberation mechanism that targets a fundamental failure mode in multi-agent LLM interactions**: agents becoming lost or drifting during prolonged multi-turn exchanges. This phenomenon has already been documented in LLM multi-turn human–model conversations, and our preliminary analysis in Fig. 3 further confirms that similar issue occurs in multi-agent settings as well. Importantly, this issue is **not specific to ReMA**. It can arise in _any_ multi-agent LLM framework where agents communicate over several turns. Our proposed restart behavior and its associated reward mechanism therefore serve as a **general mechanism** for stabilizing long-horizon multi-agent reasoning, helping agents recover from accumulated errors..

>### **(2) whether there's a risk of potentially entering modes where restarts are over-triggered**

We thank the reviewer for raising such insightful question. To address your concern, we provide a detailed analysis of the training dynamics associated with the restart behavior in Dr. MAMR. Following the experimental setting described in Sec. 6.1, we set $\alpha=\beta=0.1$, use 8 rollouts per prompt, and adopt a batch size of 128. At each global step, we track three quantities: (1) the mean reward that Dr. MAMR obtained on the training batch, (2) the total number of restart actions triggered by the reasoning agent, and (3) the average reward assigned to those restart actions. **The results are visualized in Fig. 7 in the appendix.**

From the figure, several important patterns emerge. First, as training progresses, the overall mean reward of Dr. MAMR increases steadily, and the mean reward associated specifically with restart actions exhibits a similar upward trend. This indicates that the restart reward signal is informative: it provides consistent and meaningful feedback to the reasoning agent, rather than introducing noise or instability. The agent learns to exploit the restart mechanism in a way that aligns with improved task performance.

Second, although the number of restart actions experiences a mild increase during the earliest phase of training—an expected effect due to the restart reward signal not yet being fully calibrated—this trend reverses quickly. 
After approximately 40 training steps, the number of restart actions begins to decline and eventually stabilizes around step 100. While the restart frequency does decrease, the reduction is only partial, indicating that the agent is learning to avoid unnecessary or redundant restarts. Importantly, this stabilization occurs despite the fact that the reward for restart actions continues to increase. In other words, the positive restart reward does not cause the agent to enter a degenerate mode where restarts are over-triggered simply to accumulate reward.

**This observation is precisely the behavior we aim to achieve: the reasoning agent is not “hacked” into producing restart tokens blindly. Instead, it learns when a restart is genuinely beneficial based on the current prompt and the intermediate reasoning trajectory.** 

Together, these findings provide compelling evidence that the restart mechanism in Dr. MAMR is both stable and well-behaved. **Even when rewarded positively, the model does not collapse into overuse of restart behavior. Instead, it balances restart decisions in a principled manner, demonstrating robustness and reliability in practical training conditions.**

>### Q1: Fig. 3 is also not clear. What is the "performance gap" that is being measured here? Why does the gap increase between Pass@1 and Pass@16 for AIME25/AIME24?

We thank the reviewer for pointing out this ambiguity. We clarify that in Fig. 3, the “performance gap” is defined as the difference in validation accuracy between ReMA⁺ and the original ReMA, i.e., $Gap=ValAcc(ReMA+)−ValAcc(ReMA).$
Although we stated in L320 that ReMA⁺ outperforms ReMA, we apologize for not explicitly defining this quantity in the figure.

Regarding Pass@1 vs. Pass@16, these are distinct evaluation metrics:
-   Pass@1 checks whether the model solves the problem in a single attempt.
-   Pass@16 checks whether the model solves the problem using up to 16 attempts, which provides additional opportunities for exploration and recovery from early mistakes.

And we observe that the performance gap between ReMA⁺ and ReMA increases under **Pass@16**, especially on AIME24/AIME25. Our interpretation is as follows:
-   **ReMA⁺ explicitly incentivizes the `<restart>` behavior**, allowing the reasoning agent to abandon unproductive or incorrect partial chains and explore alternative solution paths.
-   **ReMA, in contrast, tends to continue reasoning within a noisy or corrupted context once it becomes “lost,”** which limits its ability to recover even when multiple attempts are allowed.

Thus, when more attempts are permitted (Pass@16), ReMA⁺ benefits more from its improved exploration ability, leading to a larger performance advantage over ReMA. This trend is also consistent with our scaling results in Fig. 9, where the performance gap between Dr. MAMR and ReMA **widens as Pass@K increases** on the more difficult benchmarks.

    
>###  Q2: I don't understand Fig. 2. Particularly the difference from (b) to (c) to (d). What is the "causal-effect gap" here? A higher causal influence is better, yes? But it doesn't seem like there is any significant difference in the reasoning agent's causal influence from (b) to (d), for example.

>### **(1) What is the "causal-effect gap" here? A higher causal influence is better, yes?**

We thank the reviewer for this question and apologize for the lack of clarity. **The “causal-effect gap” refers to the difference between the causal influence of the meta-thinking agent and the causal influence of the reasoning agent.** Formally, it measures how imbalanced the two agents’ contributions are.

Importantly, **a higher causal influence is _not_ necessarily better.** As stated in L208 of the paper, the key problem in ReMA is that _the reasoning agent’s causal influence collapses_, while the meta-thinking agent dominates. **What we want is balanced contributions, not simply a higher value.**

>### **(2) Why (b) and (d) seem similar for the reasoning agent?**

In panel **(b)** (ReMA), we intentionally selected the _best performing checkpoint_—the point before the reasoning agent fully collapses into a lazy agent. Even at this best moment, the reasoning agent’s causal influence is much lower than the meta-thinking agent’s, revealing the persistent imbalance.

In contrast, in panel **(d)** (Dr. MAMR), although the reasoning agent’s absolute causal influence may appear numerically similar to that in (b), its relative contribution compared to the meta-thinking agent is much more balanced. This is the central improvement that our causal-influence module brings.

This distinction becomes clearer when observing training dynamics: **As shown in Fig. 4**, under standard ReMA training, the reasoning agent’s causal influence gradually collapses toward zero as training continues—demonstrating the lazy-agent failure mode. Our method prevents this collapse and keeps both agents contributing meaningfully.
